notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • The universe includes all matter, energy, space and time.
  • The universe contains galaxies, stars, planets, satellites, nebulae, black holes and other celestial objects.
  • Astronomy is the scientific study of celestial objects and the universe.
  • Cosmology is the scientific study of the origin, structure and evolution of the universe.
  • Astrophysics applies principles of physics to understand celestial objects and phenomena.
  • The observable universe is the portion of the universe from which light or other signals have had time to reach us.
  • The universe is expanding.
  • The expansion of the universe is supported by observations of distant galaxies.
  • The universe is estimated to be about 13.8 billion years old.
  • The currently accepted scientific explanation for the early evolution of the universe is the Big Bang model.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Universe → Galaxies → Stars → Planetary Systems

2. Big Bang Theory
  • The Big Bang theory explains that the universe evolved from an extremely hot and dense early state.
  • The Big Bang was not an explosion into pre-existing empty space.
  • Space itself expanded as the universe evolved.
  • The universe has continued to expand since its early stages.
  • Evidence for the Big Bang includes cosmic expansion.
  • Cosmic microwave background radiation is major evidence for the Big Bang model.
  • The observed abundance of light elements also supports the Big Bang model.
  • Hydrogen and helium formed in large quantities during the early universe.
  • Heavy elements formed later mainly inside stars and stellar explosions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Big Bang → Expanding Universe + Cosmic Microwave Background

3. Age of the Universe
  • The universe is approximately 13.8 billion years old.
  • The age of the universe is estimated using astronomical observations and cosmological models.
  • Measurements of cosmic expansion help estimate the age of the universe.
  • Cosmic microwave background observations provide important information about the early universe.
📌 Remember

Universe → About 13.8 billion years

Earth → About 4.54 billion years

4. Expansion of the Universe
  • Distant galaxies are generally observed to be moving away from us.
  • The farther a galaxy is, the greater its observed recession velocity on large scales.
  • This relationship is known as the Hubble-Lemaître law.
  • The expansion is interpreted as an expansion of space.
  • The expansion of the universe does not mean Earth is at the centre of the universe.
  • On sufficiently large scales, expansion appears similar from different locations.
5. Edwin Hubble
  • Edwin Hubble was an American astronomer.
  • He provided important observational evidence that galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way.
  • His observations showed a relationship between galaxy distance and recession velocity.
  • The Hubble Space Telescope is named after Edwin Hubble.
  • Hubble's work greatly changed scientific understanding of the scale and expansion of the universe.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Edwin Hubble → Galaxies + Expansion of Universe

6. Georges Lemaître
  • Georges Lemaître was a Belgian priest, physicist and astronomer.
  • He independently proposed an expanding universe.
  • He related galaxy recession to cosmic expansion.
  • He proposed an early form of the Big Bang idea.
  • The Hubble-Lemaître law recognises contributions of both Hubble and Lemaître.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Georges Lemaître → Expanding Universe + Early Big Bang Idea

7. Cosmic Microwave Background
  • Cosmic microwave background is abbreviated as CMB.
  • CMB is faint microwave radiation present throughout the universe.
  • It is interpreted as remnant radiation from the hot early universe.
  • CMB was discovered accidentally in 1965.
  • Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background radiation.
  • Penzias and Wilson received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1978 for their discovery.
  • CMB provides important evidence for the Big Bang model.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

CMB → Penzias + Wilson → Big Bang Evidence

8. Galaxy
  • A galaxy is a gravitationally bound system of stars, gas, dust and dark matter.
  • Galaxies may contain millions to trillions of stars.
  • Galaxies occur in groups and clusters.
  • The Milky Way is the galaxy containing the Solar System.
  • Galaxies are commonly classified as spiral, elliptical and irregular.
  • The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy.
  • Andromeda is a large spiral galaxy near the Milky Way.
  • Andromeda is also known as M31.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Solar System → Milky Way Galaxy

9. Types of Galaxies
  • Spiral galaxies have a central region and spiral arms.
  • Barred spiral galaxies have a bar-like central structure.
  • Elliptical galaxies have rounded or elongated shapes.
  • Elliptical galaxies generally contain less cold gas and dust than many spiral galaxies.
  • Irregular galaxies lack a regular spiral or elliptical form.
  • The Milky Way is classified as a barred spiral galaxy.
📌 Remember

Milky Way → Barred Spiral Galaxy

10. Milky Way Galaxy
  • The Milky Way contains the Solar System.
  • It is a barred spiral galaxy.
  • The Solar System lies in the galactic disk.
  • The Sun is located far from the galactic centre.
  • The Solar System lies in a minor spiral structure called the Orion Arm or Orion Spur.
  • The Milky Way contains hundreds of billions of stars.
  • A supermassive black hole exists at the centre of the Milky Way.
  • This central black hole is associated with Sagittarius A*.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Milky Way Centre → Sagittarius A*

11. Andromeda Galaxy
  • Andromeda is one of the nearest large galaxies to the Milky Way.
  • It is approximately 2.5 million light-years from Earth.
  • It is designated M31.
  • Andromeda and the Milky Way are members of the Local Group.
  • The Milky Way and Andromeda are gravitationally approaching each other.
12. Local Group
  • The Local Group is a collection of galaxies containing the Milky Way.
  • Andromeda is also a major member of the Local Group.
  • The Triangulum Galaxy is another notable member.
  • The Local Group contains many smaller dwarf galaxies.
  • Galaxies in the Local Group are gravitationally associated.
13. Star
  • A star is a massive luminous sphere of hot plasma held together by gravity.
  • Stars produce energy mainly through nuclear fusion.
  • Hydrogen fusion into helium powers most main-sequence stars.
  • The Sun is a star.
  • Stars differ in mass, temperature, colour, brightness and size.
  • A star's mass strongly influences its evolution.
  • Stars are born from clouds of gas and dust.
  • Stars have finite lifetimes.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Star → Nuclear Fusion → Light + Heat

14. Formation of Stars
  • Stars form in large clouds of gas and dust called nebulae.
  • Gravity causes regions of a nebula to contract.
  • A contracting region forms a protostar.
  • Temperature and pressure rise as contraction continues.
  • Nuclear fusion begins when the core becomes sufficiently hot and dense.
  • Once stable hydrogen fusion begins, the star enters the main-sequence stage.
📌 Must-Memorise Sequence

Nebula → Protostar → Main-Sequence Star

15. Nebula
  • A nebula is a large cloud of gas and dust in space.
  • Some nebulae are regions of active star formation.
  • Nebulae may appear bright or dark depending on how they interact with light.
  • Emission nebulae emit light from ionised gas.
  • Reflection nebulae reflect light from nearby stars.
  • Dark nebulae block light from objects behind them.
  • Planetary nebulae form during a late stage in the evolution of certain stars.
  • A planetary nebula has no direct relation to planets despite its name.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Planetary nebula ≠ Planet.

16. Nuclear Fusion in Stars
  • Nuclear fusion combines light nuclei to form heavier nuclei.
  • Fusion releases enormous amounts of energy.
  • In the Sun, hydrogen nuclei ultimately combine to form helium.
  • Mass is converted into energy during fusion.
  • Einstein's mass-energy relation is E = mc².
  • Nuclear fusion requires extremely high temperature and pressure.
  • Fusion in stars prevents gravitational collapse during much of their stable lifetime.
17. Main Sequence
  • Main sequence is the long stable stage in a star's life.
  • During the main sequence, hydrogen fusion occurs in the core.
  • The Sun is currently a main-sequence star.
  • Massive stars are hotter and generally consume fuel faster.
  • Low-mass stars can remain on the main sequence much longer than massive stars.
18. Colour of Stars
  • Star colour is closely related to surface temperature.
  • Blue stars are generally hotter than white stars.
  • White stars are generally hotter than yellow stars.
  • Yellow stars are generally hotter than orange and red stars.
  • Red stars are relatively cool compared with blue stars.
  • The Sun appears yellow-white and has a surface temperature of roughly 5,800 K.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Blue star → Hotter

Red star → Cooler

19. Stellar Brightness
  • Luminosity is the total energy emitted by a star per unit time.
  • Apparent brightness is how bright a star appears from Earth.
  • Apparent brightness depends on luminosity and distance.
  • A nearby faint star may appear brighter than a distant luminous star.
  • Magnitude is used to describe astronomical brightness.
  • In the magnitude system, smaller or more negative values indicate greater brightness.
20. Life Cycle of a Sun-Like Star
  • A Sun-like star begins in a nebula.
  • It forms a protostar.
  • It becomes a main-sequence star.
  • After core hydrogen is depleted, it expands into a red giant.
  • Its outer layers may be expelled as a planetary nebula.
  • The remaining core becomes a white dwarf.
  • A white dwarf gradually cools over an extremely long period.
📌 Must-Memorise Sequence

Nebula → Protostar → Main Sequence → Red Giant → Planetary Nebula → White Dwarf

21. Life Cycle of a Massive Star
  • Massive stars consume nuclear fuel more rapidly than low-mass stars.
  • A massive star can evolve into a red supergiant.
  • Its core may collapse and produce a supernova.
  • The remnant may become a neutron star.
  • A sufficiently massive remnant may become a black hole.
📌 Must-Memorise Sequence

Massive Star → Red Supergiant → Supernova → Neutron Star / Black Hole

22. Red Giant
  • A red giant is an expanded late stage in the evolution of a low- or intermediate-mass star.
  • The Sun is expected to become a red giant in the distant future.
  • Red giants have large radii.
  • Their surface temperatures are lower than those of hotter blue stars.
  • Their large size can make them highly luminous.
23. White Dwarf
  • A white dwarf is a dense stellar remnant.
  • It is the remnant core of a low- or intermediate-mass star.
  • White dwarfs no longer sustain normal core fusion.
  • They gradually cool over time.
  • A white dwarf can contain a mass comparable to the Sun in a volume comparable to Earth.
24. Chandrasekhar Limit
  • The Chandrasekhar limit is the maximum mass of a stable white dwarf supported by electron degeneracy pressure.
  • The limit is approximately 1.4 times the mass of the Sun.
  • Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar calculated the theoretical limit for white-dwarf stability.
  • A white dwarf exceeding this limit cannot remain stable in the same form.
  • Chandrasekhar received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1983.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

S. Chandrasekhar → White Dwarf → 1.4 Solar Masses → Nobel 1983

25. Supernova
  • A supernova is an extremely powerful stellar explosion.
  • Core-collapse supernovae occur at the end of the lives of massive stars.
  • Supernovae release enormous energy.
  • Supernova explosions distribute heavy elements into space.
  • Material expelled by supernovae contributes to the formation of future stars and planets.
  • Some heavy elements are produced during stellar evolution and explosive events.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Supernova → Massive Star Explosion → Heavy Elements

26. Neutron Star
  • A neutron star is an extremely dense remnant of a massive star.
  • Neutron stars are composed mainly of neutron-rich matter.
  • They may have masses greater than the Sun but radii of only about tens of kilometres.
  • Neutron stars can rotate rapidly.
  • Some rotating neutron stars emit beams of radiation observed as pulsars.
27. Pulsar
  • A pulsar is a rapidly rotating neutron star emitting beams of electromagnetic radiation.
  • Pulsars can produce highly regular pulses.
  • Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first pulsars in 1967 with Antony Hewish's research group.
  • Pulsars are not stars that physically switch on and off; the pulses result from rotating beams sweeping past Earth.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pulsar → Rotating Neutron Star

28. Black Hole
  • A black hole is a region where gravity is so strong that light cannot escape from within the event horizon.
  • Black holes can form from the collapse of sufficiently massive stars.
  • The boundary around a black hole beyond which escape is impossible is called the event horizon.
  • Black holes are detected indirectly through their effects on surrounding matter and radiation.
  • Matter falling toward a black hole may form a hot accretion disk.
  • Supermassive black holes exist at the centres of many galaxies.
  • Sagittarius A* is the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Black Hole Boundary → Event Horizon

29. Event Horizon
  • The event horizon is the boundary of a black hole.
  • Inside the event horizon, the escape velocity exceeds the speed of light.
  • Light emitted from within the event horizon cannot escape to a distant observer.
  • The event horizon is not a solid surface.
30. Solar System
  • The Solar System consists of the Sun and all objects gravitationally bound to it.
  • The Solar System formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
  • It formed from a rotating cloud of gas and dust called the solar nebula.
  • The Sun contains most of the mass of the Solar System.
  • Eight recognised planets orbit the Sun.
  • Planets orbit the Sun in elliptical paths.
  • Most planets orbit in nearly the same plane.
  • Most planets orbit the Sun in the same general direction.
📌 Must-Memorise Order

Mercury → Venus → Earth → Mars → Jupiter → Saturn → Uranus → Neptune

31. Sun
  • The Sun is the central star of the Solar System.
  • It is composed mainly of hydrogen and helium.
  • The Sun produces energy by nuclear fusion.
  • The Sun's core is the site of nuclear fusion.
  • The photosphere is the visible surface layer of the Sun.
  • The chromosphere lies above the photosphere.
  • The corona is the outer atmosphere of the Sun.
  • The corona is visible prominently during a total solar eclipse.
  • The Sun provides most of the energy driving Earth's climate and life.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sun → Hydrogen Fusion → Helium

32. Layers of the Sun
  • The core is the innermost region.
  • Nuclear fusion occurs in the core.
  • The radiative zone lies outside the core.
  • Energy moves mainly by radiation through the radiative zone.
  • The convective zone lies above the radiative zone.
  • Energy is transported by convection in the convective zone.
  • The photosphere is the visible surface.
  • The chromosphere lies above the photosphere.
  • The corona is the outermost atmosphere.
📌 Must-Memorise Sequence

Core → Radiative Zone → Convective Zone → Photosphere → Chromosphere → Corona

33. Sunspots
  • Sunspots are darker regions on the Sun's photosphere.
  • Sunspots appear dark because they are cooler than surrounding regions.
  • Sunspots are associated with strong magnetic fields.
  • Sunspot numbers vary in an approximately 11-year solar cycle.
  • Increased solar activity is associated with more frequent sunspots and solar eruptions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Sunspot Cycle → About 11 years

34. Solar Flare
  • A solar flare is a sudden release of energy in the Sun's atmosphere.
  • Solar flares are associated with magnetic activity.
  • They can emit intense electromagnetic radiation.
  • Strong solar activity can affect radio communication and satellites.
  • Solar flares may occur along with coronal mass ejections.
35. Solar Wind
  • Solar wind is a stream of charged particles emitted from the Sun.
  • Solar wind interacts with Earth's magnetic field.
  • Earth's magnetosphere helps shield the planet from much of the solar wind.
  • Solar-wind interactions contribute to auroras.
36. Aurora
  • Aurora is a natural light display in the upper atmosphere.
  • It occurs when charged particles interact with gases in Earth's atmosphere.
  • Auroras are common near polar regions.
  • Aurora Borealis is the Northern Lights.
  • Aurora Australis is the Southern Lights.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aurora Borealis → Northern Hemisphere

Aurora Australis → Southern Hemisphere

37. Planets
  • A planet is a celestial body orbiting a star.
  • The Solar System has eight recognised planets.
  • The inner planets are Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars.
  • The outer planets are Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
  • Inner planets are also called terrestrial planets.
  • Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants.
  • Uranus and Neptune are commonly called ice giants.
  • Planets do not produce visible light through normal nuclear fusion like stars.
38. Terrestrial Planets
  • Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are terrestrial planets.
  • Terrestrial planets are relatively small and rocky.
  • They have solid surfaces.
  • They are located in the inner Solar System.
  • They generally have fewer moons than the giant planets.
  • They do not possess large ring systems like the giant planets.
📌 Remember

Terrestrial → Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars

39. Giant Planets
  • Jupiter is the largest planet.
  • Saturn is the second-largest planet.
  • Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants.
  • Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
  • Giant planets have thick atmospheres.
  • All four giant planets possess ring systems.
  • Giant planets have many natural satellites.
40. Mercury
  • Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.
  • Mercury is the smallest planet in the Solar System.
  • Mercury has no natural satellite.
  • Mercury has a very thin exosphere rather than a dense atmosphere.
  • Its surface is heavily cratered.
  • Mercury completes one orbit around the Sun in about 88 Earth days.
  • Mercury experiences very large temperature variations between day and night.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mercury → Closest + Smallest + No Moon

41. Venus
  • Venus is the second planet from the Sun.
  • Venus is similar to Earth in size.
  • Venus has a dense atmosphere dominated by carbon dioxide.
  • Venus has a strong greenhouse effect.
  • Venus has the highest average surface temperature of any planet in the Solar System.
  • Venus is hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun.
  • Venus has no natural satellite.
  • Venus rotates very slowly.
  • Venus rotates in the opposite direction to most planets.
  • Venus is commonly called Earth's twin because of similarities in size and mass.
  • Venus is often visible as a bright morning or evening object.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Hottest planet → Venus

Closest to Sun → Mercury

42. Earth
  • Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
  • Earth is the only known planet with life.
  • Liquid water covers most of Earth's surface.
  • Earth's atmosphere is dominated by nitrogen and oxygen.
  • Earth has one natural satellite, the Moon.
  • Earth's rotation produces day and night.
  • Earth's revolution around the Sun defines the year.
  • Earth's axial tilt is responsible for seasonal variation.
  • Earth's magnetic field helps protect the planet from charged solar particles.
43. Mars
  • Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.
  • Mars is called the Red Planet.
  • Its reddish colour is due mainly to iron oxides on the surface.
  • Mars has a thin atmosphere dominated by carbon dioxide.
  • Mars has two small moons: Phobos and Deimos.
  • Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest known volcano in the Solar System.
  • Valles Marineris is a vast canyon system on Mars.
  • Evidence indicates that liquid water existed on ancient Mars.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mars → Red Planet → Phobos + Deimos

44. Jupiter
  • Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun.
  • Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System.
  • It is a gas giant.
  • Jupiter is composed mainly of hydrogen and helium.
  • The Great Red Spot is a giant storm in Jupiter's atmosphere.
  • Jupiter has a strong magnetic field.
  • Jupiter has a faint ring system.
  • Ganymede, a moon of Jupiter, is the largest natural satellite in the Solar System.
  • Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto are the four large Galilean moons.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Jupiter → Largest Planet → Great Red Spot

45. Galilean Satellites
  • Galileo Galilei observed four large moons of Jupiter in 1610.
  • They are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
  • These are collectively called the Galilean satellites.
  • Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System.
  • Europa is of scientific interest because evidence suggests a subsurface ocean beneath its icy crust.
📌 Must-Memorise

Io → Europa → Ganymede → Callisto

46. Saturn
  • Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun.
  • Saturn is the second-largest planet.
  • It is a gas giant.
  • Saturn is famous for its prominent ring system.
  • The rings consist mainly of ice particles, rock and dust.
  • Saturn's average density is less than that of water.
  • Titan is Saturn's largest moon.
  • Titan has a dense atmosphere.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Saturn → Prominent Rings → Titan

47. Uranus
  • Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun.
  • Uranus is an ice giant.
  • Uranus appears blue-green mainly because methane in its atmosphere absorbs red light.
  • Uranus has a ring system.
  • Uranus rotates with an extreme axial tilt.
  • It appears to rotate almost on its side.
  • Uranus was discovered by William Herschel in 1781.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Uranus → William Herschel → 1781

48. Neptune
  • Neptune is the eighth planet from the Sun.
  • Neptune is the farthest recognised major planet from the Sun.
  • It is an ice giant.
  • Neptune's atmosphere contains hydrogen, helium and methane.
  • Neptune has extremely strong winds.
  • Triton is Neptune's largest moon.
  • Neptune was predicted mathematically before it was observed telescopically.
  • It was discovered observationally in 1846.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Neptune → Eighth + Farthest Major Planet

49. Dwarf Planets
  • A dwarf planet orbits the Sun.
  • It is approximately round due to its own gravity.
  • It has not cleared other objects from its orbital neighbourhood.
  • Pluto is classified as a dwarf planet.
  • Pluto was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
  • The International Astronomical Union is abbreviated as IAU.
  • Other recognised dwarf planets include Ceres, Eris, Haumea and Makemake.
  • Ceres lies in the asteroid belt.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pluto → Dwarf Planet → 2006 → IAU

50. Pluto
  • Pluto was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh.
  • Pluto was originally classified as the ninth planet.
  • It was reclassified as a dwarf planet in 2006.
  • Pluto lies in the Kuiper Belt region.
  • Charon is Pluto's largest moon.
  • Pluto's orbit is more eccentric and inclined than those of the eight major planets.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Clyde Tombaugh → Pluto → 1930

51. Natural Satellites
  • A natural satellite is a celestial body that naturally orbits a planet or dwarf planet.
  • Earth's natural satellite is the Moon.
  • Mercury and Venus have no natural satellites.
  • Giant planets possess many natural satellites.
  • Ganymede is the largest natural satellite in the Solar System.
  • Titan is the largest moon of Saturn.
  • Triton is the largest moon of Neptune.
52. Moon
  • The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite.
  • The Moon does not produce its own visible light.
  • It shines by reflecting sunlight.
  • The Moon's gravitational pull contributes strongly to ocean tides.
  • The Moon rotates on its axis.
  • The Moon revolves around Earth.
  • Its rotation period is approximately equal to its orbital period.
  • Therefore, nearly the same side of the Moon always faces Earth.
  • The far side of the Moon is not permanently dark.
  • The Moon has virtually no substantial atmosphere.
  • Its surface contains craters, mountains and plains called maria.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Far side of Moon ≠ Dark side permanently.

53. Phases of the Moon
  • Moon phases result from changing geometry between the Sun, Earth and Moon.
  • New Moon occurs when the Moon is approximately between Earth and the Sun.
  • Full Moon occurs when Earth is approximately between the Sun and Moon.
  • First quarter and third quarter are intermediate phases.
  • Moon phases are not caused by Earth's shadow.
  • Earth's shadow is involved specifically in a lunar eclipse.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Moon phases ≠ Earth's shadow.

54. Tides
  • Tides are periodic changes in sea level.
  • The Moon's gravity is the major cause of Earth's tides.
  • The Sun also contributes to tides.
  • Spring tides occur around New Moon and Full Moon.
  • During spring tides, the gravitational effects of Sun and Moon reinforce each other.
  • Neap tides occur around first and third quarter phases.
  • During neap tides, the Sun and Moon exert tidal effects in roughly perpendicular directions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Spring Tide → New Moon + Full Moon

Neap Tide → First Quarter + Third Quarter

55. Rotation and Revolution
  • Rotation is the spinning of a body about its axis.
  • Revolution is the orbital movement of a body around another body.
  • Earth rotates from west to east.
  • Earth completes one rotation in approximately 24 hours.
  • Rotation causes day and night.
  • Earth completes one revolution around the Sun in approximately 365¼ days.
  • Revolution combined with axial tilt produces seasonal changes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Rotation → Day and Night

Revolution + Axial Tilt → Seasons

56. Earth's Axis and Seasons
  • Earth's rotational axis is tilted about 23.5° relative to the perpendicular to its orbital plane.
  • Seasonal changes result mainly from Earth's axial tilt and revolution.
  • Seasons are not caused primarily by changes in Earth's distance from the Sun.
  • When the Northern Hemisphere is tilted toward the Sun, it receives more direct sunlight and longer days.
  • At the same time, the Southern Hemisphere experiences the opposite season.
57. Equinox
  • Equinox occurs when day and night are approximately equal in length worldwide.
  • Equinoxes occur twice each year.
  • The March equinox occurs around 20 or 21 March.
  • The September equinox occurs around 22 or 23 September.
  • At equinox, the Sun is approximately overhead at the equator.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Equinox → Nearly Equal Day and Night

58. Solstice
  • Solstices occur when the Sun reaches its greatest apparent northward or southward position.
  • The June solstice occurs around 21 June.
  • The December solstice occurs around 21 or 22 December.
  • June solstice gives the longest day in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • December solstice gives the shortest day in the Northern Hemisphere.
  • Seasonal conditions are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere.
59. Solar Eclipse
  • A solar eclipse occurs when the Moon comes between the Sun and Earth.
  • The Moon's shadow falls on Earth during a solar eclipse.
  • Solar eclipses occur only near New Moon.
  • A total solar eclipse occurs when the Sun is completely covered from the observer's location.
  • A partial solar eclipse occurs when only part of the Sun is covered.
  • An annular solar eclipse occurs when the Moon appears smaller than the Sun and leaves a bright ring.
  • The bright ring seen during an annular eclipse is often called a ring of fire.
  • A solar eclipse does not occur at every New Moon because the Moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbital plane.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Solar Eclipse → Sun–Moon–Earth → New Moon

60. Lunar Eclipse
  • A lunar eclipse occurs when Earth comes between the Sun and Moon.
  • Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.
  • Lunar eclipses occur only near Full Moon.
  • A total lunar eclipse occurs when the entire Moon enters Earth's umbra.
  • During some total lunar eclipses, the Moon appears reddish.
  • The reddish colour occurs because Earth's atmosphere scatters and refracts sunlight into Earth's shadow.
  • A lunar eclipse can be seen from a much larger region of Earth than a total solar eclipse.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lunar Eclipse → Sun–Earth–Moon → Full Moon

61. Umbra and Penumbra
  • Umbra is the darkest central part of a shadow.
  • Penumbra is the lighter outer region of a shadow.
  • Total eclipse conditions occur in the umbral region.
  • Partial eclipse conditions occur in the penumbral region.
📌 Remember

Umbra → Dark central shadow

Penumbra → Partial outer shadow

62. Asteroid
  • Asteroids are small rocky or metallic bodies orbiting the Sun.
  • Most known asteroids are concentrated in the asteroid belt.
  • The main asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
  • Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt and is classified as a dwarf planet.
  • Asteroids are remnants from the early Solar System.
  • Some asteroids have orbits that approach Earth.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Asteroid Belt → Between Mars and Jupiter

63. Comet
  • A comet is a small icy body orbiting the Sun.
  • Comets contain frozen gases, dust and rocky material.
  • When a comet approaches the Sun, heating produces a glowing coma.
  • A comet may develop one or more tails.
  • Comet tails generally point away from the Sun.
  • Solar radiation and solar wind influence comet tails.
  • Many comets have highly elliptical orbits.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Comet tail → Points away from Sun, not necessarily behind the comet's direction of motion.

64. Halley's Comet
  • Halley's Comet is a famous periodic comet.
  • It returns to the inner Solar System approximately every 76 years.
  • Edmond Halley predicted its periodic return using Newtonian mechanics.
  • The comet was named after Edmond Halley.
  • Halley's Comet was last visible from Earth in 1986.
  • Its next perihelion is expected in 2061.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Halley's Comet → About 76 years

65. Meteoroid, Meteor and Meteorite
  • A meteoroid is a small rocky or metallic body travelling through space.
  • A meteor is the streak of light produced when a meteoroid enters Earth's atmosphere and heats up.
  • A meteorite is material that survives passage through the atmosphere and reaches Earth's surface.
  • Meteors are commonly called shooting stars.
  • Shooting stars are not actual stars.
📌 Must-Memorise

Meteoroid → In space

Meteor → Burning in atmosphere

Meteorite → Reaches ground

66. Meteor Shower
  • A meteor shower occurs when Earth passes through a stream of debris.
  • Comets are the source of many meteor-shower debris streams.
  • Many meteors appear to originate from a common point called the radiant.
  • Meteor showers occur at predictable times each year.
67. Kuiper Belt
  • The Kuiper Belt is a region beyond Neptune.
  • It contains many icy objects.
  • Pluto is a Kuiper Belt object.
  • The Kuiper Belt is a source region for many short-period comets.
  • It is part of the outer Solar System.
68. Oort Cloud
  • The Oort Cloud is a hypothesised distant reservoir of icy bodies surrounding the Solar System.
  • It is believed to be a source of many long-period comets.
  • The Oort Cloud lies much farther from the Sun than the Kuiper Belt.
  • Its existence is inferred from comet orbits.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kuiper Belt → Short-period comets

Oort Cloud → Long-period comets

69. Astronomical Unit
  • Astronomical Unit is abbreviated as AU.
  • One AU is approximately the average distance between Earth and the Sun.
  • One AU is about 149.6 million kilometres.
  • AU is useful for measuring distances within the Solar System.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 AU → Earth–Sun Average Distance → ~149.6 million km

70. Light-Year
  • A light-year is the distance light travels in vacuum in one year.
  • It is a unit of distance.
  • One light-year is approximately 9.46 trillion kilometres.
  • Light-year is useful for measuring distances between stars and galaxies.
  • Light travels at approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Light-year → Distance, not time.

71. Parsec
  • Parsec is an astronomical unit of distance.
  • One parsec is approximately 3.26 light-years.
  • Parsec is based on stellar parallax.
  • Astronomers frequently express stellar and galactic distances in parsecs.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 parsec → ~3.26 light-years

72. Stellar Parallax
  • Stellar parallax is the apparent shift in position of a nearby star against distant background stars.
  • It results from Earth's changing position as it orbits the Sun.
  • Parallax is used to determine distances to nearby stars.
  • Greater parallax corresponds to a nearer star.
  • Smaller parallax corresponds to a more distant star.
73. Constellation
  • A constellation is a recognised region or apparent pattern of stars in the sky.
  • Stars in a constellation may lie at very different distances from Earth.
  • Constellations are apparent patterns as seen from Earth.
  • The International Astronomical Union officially recognises 88 constellations.
  • Orion is a well-known constellation.
  • Ursa Major is another prominent constellation.
74. Pole Star
  • Polaris is commonly called the Pole Star or North Star.
  • Polaris lies close to the direction of Earth's north rotational axis.
  • It appears nearly fixed in the northern sky.
  • Polaris has historically been useful for navigation.
  • Polaris is part of the constellation Ursa Minor.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Polaris → North Star → Ursa Minor

75. Saptarishi
  • Saptarishi commonly refers to seven prominent stars of Ursa Major in Indian tradition.
  • Ursa Major is also known as the Great Bear.
  • The prominent seven-star pattern is called the Big Dipper in North America.
  • The pointer stars of the Big Dipper can help locate Polaris.
76. Zodiac
  • The zodiac is a band of the sky around the ecliptic.
  • The Sun, Moon and planets appear to move through this region from Earth's perspective.
  • Astronomy scientifically studies the positions and motions of these objects.
  • Astrology assigns supposed human influences to zodiac positions but lacks established scientific evidence.
77. Geocentric Model
  • The geocentric model places Earth at the centre of the universe or planetary system.
  • Claudius Ptolemy developed a highly influential geocentric astronomical model.
  • Ptolemy's model was used for many centuries.
  • The geocentric model was later replaced by more accurate heliocentric descriptions of the Solar System.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Ptolemy → Geocentric Model

78. Heliocentric Model
  • The heliocentric model places the Sun near the centre of the planetary system.
  • Nicolaus Copernicus developed a major heliocentric model in the 16th century.
  • Copernicus proposed that Earth rotates on its axis and revolves around the Sun.
  • The heliocentric model simplified understanding of planetary motions.
  • Later observations and mathematical work strengthened the heliocentric framework.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Copernicus → Heliocentric Model

79. Galileo Galilei
  • Galileo Galilei used a telescope for astronomical observations.
  • In 1610 he reported observations of four large moons orbiting Jupiter.
  • These observations showed that not everything in the heavens orbited Earth.
  • Galileo observed phases of Venus.
  • The phases of Venus provided strong evidence supporting heliocentric planetary arrangements.
  • Galileo also observed mountains and craters on the Moon.
  • He observed sunspots.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Galileo → Telescope → Jupiter's Moons + Phases of Venus

80. Johannes Kepler
  • Johannes Kepler formulated three laws of planetary motion.
  • Kepler showed that planets move in elliptical orbits.
  • The Sun lies at one focus of a planetary ellipse.
  • A line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times.
  • The square of a planet's orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis of its orbit.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kepler → Laws of Planetary Motion → Elliptical Orbits

81. Kepler's First Law
  • Planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits.
  • The Sun occupies one focus of the ellipse.
  • Planetary orbits are not perfect circles.
📌 Remember

Kepler I → Ellipse

82. Kepler's Second Law
  • A line joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time.
  • A planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun.
  • A planet moves slower when it is farther from the Sun.
📌 Remember

Kepler II → Equal Areas in Equal Times

83. Kepler's Third Law
  • The square of the orbital period is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis.
  • In symbolic form, T² ∝ a³ for bodies orbiting the same central mass.
  • More distant planets generally take longer to orbit the Sun.
📌 Remember

Kepler III → T² ∝ a³

84. Isaac Newton and Astronomy
  • Isaac Newton formulated the laws of motion.
  • Newton formulated the law of universal gravitation.
  • Newton's gravitational theory explained planetary motion.
  • Newton showed that the same gravitational law applies on Earth and in the heavens.
  • Newton's work provided a physical explanation for Kepler's planetary laws.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newton → Universal Gravitation → Planetary Motion

85. Universal Gravitation
  • Every mass attracts every other mass.
  • Gravitational force is directly proportional to the product of the masses.
  • Gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between their centres.
  • Universal gravitation is expressed as F = Gm₁m₂/r².
  • G is the universal gravitational constant.
  • Gravity keeps planets in orbit around the Sun.
  • Gravity keeps natural satellites in orbit around planets.
86. Escape Velocity
  • Escape velocity is the minimum speed needed to escape the gravitational influence of a body without further propulsion.
  • Earth's escape velocity is approximately 11.2 km/s from the surface, ignoring atmospheric resistance.
  • Escape velocity depends on the mass and radius of the celestial body.
  • A more massive or more compact body generally has a higher escape velocity.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Earth Escape Velocity → ~11.2 km/s

87. Artificial Satellite
  • An artificial satellite is a human-made object placed in orbit.
  • Satellites are used for communication.
  • Satellites are used for weather monitoring.
  • Satellites are used for remote sensing.
  • Satellites are used for navigation.
  • Satellites are used for scientific research.
  • Artificial satellites remain in orbit because of the balance between forward motion and gravitational attraction.
88. Geostationary Satellite
  • A geostationary satellite appears fixed over one point on Earth's equator.
  • It orbits in the same direction as Earth's rotation.
  • Its orbital period equals Earth's rotational period.
  • A geostationary satellite must orbit above the equator.
  • Geostationary orbit is approximately 35,786 km above Earth's equator.
  • Geostationary satellites are useful for communication and weather observation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Geostationary → Equatorial Orbit → ~35,786 km

89. Polar Satellite
  • Polar satellites travel in orbits passing near Earth's poles.
  • As Earth rotates beneath them, polar satellites can observe much of Earth's surface.
  • Polar orbits are useful for remote sensing and Earth observation.
  • Many resource-mapping and environmental-monitoring satellites use near-polar or sun-synchronous orbits.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Geostationary → Communication / fixed apparent position

Polar → Earth observation / global coverage

90. Indian Space Programme
  • ISRO stands for Indian Space Research Organisation.
  • ISRO was established in 1969.
  • Vikram Sarabhai is widely regarded as the father of the Indian space programme.
  • ISRO headquarters is in Bengaluru.
  • India's space programme focuses on communication, remote sensing, navigation, scientific research and exploration.
  • The Department of Space is responsible for India's space programme.
  • The Space Commission and Department of Space were established in 1972.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vikram Sarabhai → Indian Space Programme

ISRO → 1969

91. Aryabhata Satellite
  • Aryabhata was India's first satellite.
  • It was launched on 19 April 1975.
  • It was named after the ancient Indian mathematician and astronomer Aryabhata.
  • Aryabhata was launched by the Soviet Union.
  • The satellite marked an important milestone in India's space programme.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

First Indian Satellite → Aryabhata → 1975

92. Rohini Satellite
  • Rohini Satellite RS-1 was placed into orbit in 1980.
  • It was launched using India's Satellite Launch Vehicle-3.
  • SLV-3 was India's first experimental satellite launch vehicle.
  • The successful Rohini launch demonstrated India's indigenous satellite-launch capability.
  • A. P. J. Abdul Kalam was closely associated with the SLV-3 programme.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rohini → SLV-3 → 1980

93. Launch Vehicles
  • A launch vehicle carries satellites or spacecraft from Earth into space.
  • PSLV stands for Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle.
  • GSLV stands for Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle.
  • PSLV has been extensively used for Earth-observation and other satellite missions.
  • GSLV is designed to place heavier payloads into higher-energy orbits.
  • Cryogenic propulsion is important in high-energy upper stages of certain launch vehicles.
94. Chandrayaan Missions
  • Chandrayaan refers to India's lunar exploration programme.
  • Chandrayaan-1 was India's first lunar mission.
  • Chandrayaan-1 was launched in 2008.
  • Chandrayaan-1 provided important evidence of water/hydroxyl molecules on the lunar surface.
  • Chandrayaan-2 was launched in 2019.
  • Chandrayaan-2 included an orbiter, lander and rover.
  • Chandrayaan-3 achieved a successful soft landing on the Moon in 2023.
  • India's lunar exploration missions are operated by ISRO.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Chandrayaan-1 → 2008 → Moon

Chandrayaan-3 → Successful Soft Landing → 2023

95. Mangalyaan
  • Mars Orbiter Mission is commonly called Mangalyaan.
  • It was India's first interplanetary mission.
  • Mangalyaan was launched in 2013.
  • It entered Mars orbit in 2014.
  • India became the first country to reach Mars orbit successfully on its first attempt.
  • ISRO conducted the mission.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mangalyaan → Mars Orbiter Mission → 2013 launch → 2014 Mars orbit

96. Aditya-L1
  • Aditya-L1 is India's solar-observation mission.
  • It is designed to study the Sun.
  • The spacecraft operates around the Sun-Earth L1 region.
  • L1 provides a useful location for continuous solar observation.
  • Aditya-L1 studies the solar corona, solar wind and related phenomena.
  • It is India's first dedicated solar observatory mission.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aditya-L1 → Sun

97. Lagrange Points
  • Lagrange points are locations where gravitational and orbital effects allow a spacecraft to maintain a relatively stable position with respect to two large bodies.
  • There are five principal Lagrange points, L1 to L5, in a two-body system.
  • The Sun-Earth L1 point lies between Earth and the Sun.
  • L1 is useful for continuous observation of the Sun.
  • Aditya-L1 operates in a halo orbit around the Sun-Earth L1 point.
98. Important Indian Astronomers
  • Aryabhata was an ancient Indian mathematician and astronomer.
  • Aryabhata wrote the Aryabhatiya.
  • Aryabhata explained that the apparent daily motion of stars is related to Earth's rotation.
  • Varahamihira was an important ancient Indian astronomer and mathematician.
  • Brahmagupta made major contributions to mathematics and astronomy.
  • Bhaskara II was an important Indian mathematician and astronomer.
  • Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar made major contributions to stellar astrophysics.
99. Aryabhata
  • Aryabhata was born in 476 CE.
  • His major work is the Aryabhatiya.
  • He gave important astronomical and mathematical explanations.
  • He recognised Earth's rotation.
  • He gave scientific explanations for eclipses based on shadows.
  • India's first satellite was named Aryabhata in his honour.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Aryabhata → Aryabhatiya → Earth's Rotation + Eclipse Explanation

100. Must-Memorise Planet Facts
  • Closest planet to Sun → Mercury.
  • Smallest planet → Mercury.
  • Hottest planet → Venus.
  • Earth's twin → Venus.
  • Red Planet → Mars.
  • Largest planet → Jupiter.
  • Great Red Spot → Jupiter.
  • Largest moon → Ganymede.
  • Most prominent ring system → Saturn.
  • Saturn's largest moon → Titan.
  • Planet rotating nearly on its side → Uranus.
  • Farthest major planet → Neptune.
  • Dwarf planet formerly ninth planet → Pluto.
  • Planet with no moon → Mercury and Venus.
  • Earth has → One Moon.
  • Mars has → Phobos and Deimos.
101. Must-Memorise Astronomy Units
  • Astronomical Unit → Average Earth-Sun distance.
  • 1 AU → About 149.6 million km.
  • Light-year → Distance travelled by light in one year.
  • 1 light-year → About 9.46 trillion km.
  • Parsec → Astronomical distance unit.
  • 1 parsec → About 3.26 light-years.
  • Speed of light → Approximately 3 × 10⁸ m/s.
102. Important Astronomers and Discoveries
  • Ptolemy → Geocentric system.
  • Copernicus → Heliocentric system.
  • Galileo → Telescopic astronomy and Galilean satellites.
  • Johannes Kepler → Planetary-motion laws.
  • Isaac Newton → Universal gravitation.
  • William Herschel → Discovery of Uranus.
  • Clyde Tombaugh → Discovery of Pluto.
  • Edwin Hubble → Galaxies and cosmic expansion.
  • Georges Lemaître → Expanding universe and early Big Bang model.
  • Penzias and Wilson → Cosmic microwave background.
  • S. Chandrasekhar → Chandrasekhar limit.
  • Jocelyn Bell Burnell → Discovery of pulsars.
  • Edmond Halley → Predicted return of Halley's Comet.
103. TNPSC Traps
  • Universe and Solar System are not the same.
  • Solar System is only a tiny part of the Milky Way.
  • Milky Way is a galaxy, not the entire universe.
  • The Sun is a star.
  • Planets reflect sunlight; they do not shine like stars through normal nuclear fusion.
  • Blue stars are hotter than red stars.
  • A light-year is a unit of distance.
  • One parsec is greater than one light-year.
  • Mercury is closest to the Sun.
  • Venus is the hottest planet.
  • Jupiter is the largest planet.
  • Saturn is not the only planet with rings.
  • All four giant planets possess rings.
  • Mercury and Venus have no moons.
  • Ganymede is larger than Earth's Moon.
  • Pluto is a dwarf planet.
  • Ceres is also a dwarf planet.
  • Asteroid belt lies between Mars and Jupiter.
  • Comet tails generally point away from the Sun.
  • Meteoroid, meteor and meteorite are different.
  • Moon phases are not caused by Earth's shadow.
  • Solar eclipse occurs near New Moon.
  • Lunar eclipse occurs near Full Moon.
  • Spring tides occur at New Moon and Full Moon.
  • Seasons are not caused mainly by Earth's changing distance from the Sun.
  • Geostationary satellites orbit above the equator.
  • Polar satellites are particularly useful for Earth observation.
  • Astronomy is a science; astrology is not an established scientific discipline.
104. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Big Bang → Early hot dense universe.
  • CMB → Big Bang evidence.
  • Hubble → Expansion.
  • Milky Way → Barred spiral.
  • Sun → Star.
  • Star → Nuclear fusion.
  • Nebula → Star-forming cloud.
  • Sun-like star → White dwarf.
  • Massive star → Supernova.
  • Pulsar → Rotating neutron star.
  • Black hole → Event horizon.
  • Solar System → 8 planets.
  • Mercury → Closest + Smallest.
  • Venus → Hottest.
  • Earth → Life.
  • Mars → Red.
  • Jupiter → Largest.
  • Saturn → Rings.
  • Uranus → Sideways rotation.
  • Neptune → Farthest major planet.
  • Pluto → Dwarf planet.
  • Asteroid belt → Mars-Jupiter.
  • Halley → ~76 years.
  • Meteoroid → Space.
  • Meteor → Atmosphere.
  • Meteorite → Ground.
  • AU → Earth-Sun distance.
  • Light-year → Distance.
  • Parsec → 3.26 light-years.
  • Copernicus → Heliocentric.
  • Kepler → Elliptical orbits.
  • Newton → Gravitation.
  • Aryabhata → First Indian satellite, 1975.
  • Mangalyaan → Mars.
  • Chandrayaan → Moon.
  • Aditya-L1 → Sun.
